summary:
New York sits in the fifteen-state "Most Protective" tier of a July 2026 national legal-risk ranking built from a rubric applied to thousands of tracked anti-trans bills, covering youth-care bans, bathroom bans, birth-certificate and driver's-licence restrictions and the withdrawal of legal recognition. The same ranking places the least protective states at the opposite end, with prison terms of up to five years for youth-care provision and arrest policies for gender-identity bathroom use.

Gender identity and expression have been protected statewide in credit, housing, employment, education and public accommodations since the Gender Expression Non-Discrimination Act took effect in February 2019. That statute built on a 16 December 2009 executive order barring state agencies from gender-identity discrimination across hiring, termination, retention, appointment, promotion, tenure, recruitment and compensation, and on Division of Human Rights regulations issued 4 November 2015 and effective 20 January 2016 prohibiting transgender harassment and discrimination in those domains. A 2024 constitutional amendment explicitly bans discrimination on the basis of gender identity.

The Hate Crimes Act has covered gender identity and expression since 1 November 2019, with further anti-bias reform bills signed in November 2022. The gay and transgender panic defence was repealed in June 2019 with immediate effect, and conversion therapy on minors has been banned since 25 January 2019.

New York operates a shield or refuge law for gender-affirming care, listed as in force in equality-mapping data as of 27 September 2026. It protects patients and providers from civil or criminal charges when care that is legal in New York has been banned in the patient's home state, which bears directly on visitors travelling from states with youth-care bans.

Custody exposure is addressed by a shield statute of 25 June 2023, which bars New York courts from enforcing out-of-state orders that remove custody over youth gender-affirming care, bars treating that care as child abuse, and bars law-enforcement cooperation with out-of-state agencies. A New York City executive order of 12 June 2023 bars city resources from being used to detain, prosecute or investigate the provision or receipt of gender-affirming care; an Ithaca ordinance followed in September 2023 and City Council bills expanding provider protections were introduced in April 2025.

Identity documents are comparatively open. Since 2014 transgender adults have been able to change the gender on a New York birth certificate by notarized medical affidavit verifying surgery or a gender dysphoria diagnosis; a 2020 revision allows self-affirmation at 17 or older and change with parental consent below that age. The June 2021 Gender Recognition Act allowed an X marker on driver's licences and eased sealing of name and gender-change records. An X marker took effect on New York City birth certificates on 1 January 2019, on death certificates from 2 January 2020, was reported for state court and jury documents in November 2019 and in healthcare data from August 2020, and was approved for all state forms in April 2022 for 2023.

A law signed in December 2020 and effective 23 March 2021 mandates gender-neutral bathrooms. New York operates no state bathroom ban of the kind in force in nine states and one territory elsewhere, where trans use of facilities is restricted in schools or government buildings and in some cases made a criminal offence.

Nassau County is the one local exception: it bans transgender athletes from women's sports on county-run facilities. A 2025 ruling found no clear violation of anti-discrimination law in that ban, and a civil-liberties lawsuit seeking inclusion remains the mechanism challenging it.

Enforcement machinery has been reformed rather than turned against trans people. Former Penal Law Section 240.37, in force since 1976 and used by police to harass and arrest transgender individuals, was repealed in February 2021 with immediate effect. The 2009 executive order defines gender identity to include having or being perceived as having a gender identity, self-image, appearance, behaviour or expression whether or not different from sex assigned at birth, and requires equal-opportunity efforts, consistent guidelines and swift confidential investigation of complaints.

Sector-specific protections round out the position: the state anti-bullying law covers gender including gender identity and expression, including cyberbullying, in all public elementary and secondary schools, with a loophole closed in 2019; a June 2023 law explicitly includes gender identity in drug treatment and addiction programs; a November 2020 law requires annual judiciary statistics broken down by gender identity; and a November 2021 law effective 1 January 2022 requires utilities and municipalities to use residents' preferred names and pronouns.

Marriages are recognised without regard to the partners' sex under the Marriage Equality Act, in effect since 24 July 2011, so a trans visitor in a relationship that would be locally classed as same-sex can marry in New York and have that marriage recognised.
tangentialFactors:
The July 2026 ranking that places New York in the top tier is a rubric applied to tracked legislation rather than a measure of incidents or reported violence, so it describes the state of the law and the direction of legislatures, not the frequency of anything a visitor might encounter. Its contrast tier is drawn from other states in the country, where youth-care bans carry prison terms of up to five years and gender-identity bathroom use can trigger arrest.

New York's shield architecture is one of a minority nationally: equality-mapping data as of 27 September 2026 records shields in sixteen states and the District of Columbia, covering 38% of trans people aged 13 and over, against thirty-two states and five territories holding none. The figure explains why the New York shield law is visitor-relevant rather than boilerplate: a large share of domestic travellers arrive from jurisdictions without any.

New York City is reported to have the largest transgender population in the country, estimated at 50,000 in 2018 and concentrated in Manhattan and Queens. That is a raw count with no population denominator attached in the source, so it indicates the scale of visible community infrastructure rather than any comparative risk level.

The state's protections are not uniform at county level. Nassau County's ban on transgender athletes using county-run facilities for women's sports shows that a protective statewide framework can coexist with restrictive local policy on publicly operated venues.

outOfScopeNotes:
Most of the statutory detail in this record rests on a single encyclopedic compilation rather than on the text of the New York statutes themselves; dates, effective provisions and section numbers are reported as sourced and are not independently verified here.

The status of the Nassau County litigation is unresolved. The 2025 ruling that the county ban did not clearly violate anti-discrimination law is reported, but no later judgment, settlement or injunction is sourced, so the ban should be treated as in force unless confirmed otherwise.

The April 2025 New York City Council bills expanding provider protections are reported as introduced. Whether they were enacted, amended or stalled is not sourced, and their current effect is unresolved.

The July 2026 tier ranking is described by its publisher as rubric-based over tracked bills. The rubric's weighting, its treatment of enforcement as distinct from enactment, and any per-capita adjustment are not published in the material reviewed, so the tier indicates legal posture rather than measured outcomes.

The sources reviewed provide no transgender-specific measure of societal tolerance distinct from LGBTQ-general language, and the polling they carry covers sexual orientation and gender identity together. Nothing in this record supports a claim about how a trans visitor will be received socially in New York beyond what the legal protections imply.

This record covers New York state and local measures only. Federal document, entry and screening rules are carried by the national record and are not assessed here.
